1:
The accession itself is reported without dispute. Clarke reads the clause about the people of Judah to mean that they all agreed to place this son on his father's throne, and Gill passes the verses over to the parallel account, where the same king is called Azariah. Clarke notes in the same breath that this king is called by several different names, and Ellicott settles what that variation is worth.

His case is that the two names are both genuine. This writer always calls him Uzziah, with a single exception in the genealogies; the book of Kings uses Azariah in several places and Uzziah in several others, and the Greek of Kings reads Azariah throughout, which makes that book's usage uniform where the Hebrew is not; Uzziah is also the form standing in the headings of three of the prophets. The variation is not therefore to be treated either as a popular abbreviation or as a transcriber's blunder, as Schrader and others have suggested. Ellicott then brings external evidence, that in the Assyrian inscriptions of Tiglathpileser this king is uniformly called by the longer name. Clearly, he concludes, he was known by both, but to foreigners chiefly by the second; and he compares another pair of names in the same book which interchange the same way.

On the building at the port the comments are brief and converge. Ellicott gives the emphatic rendering, that it was he who built the place, identifies it with the form the parallel uses, and locates it as the Idumean port on the Red Sea; Clarke sends the reader to the parallel for the same identification. Ellicott adds the observation that governs the whole opening of the chapter, that the first four verses are identical with the parallel in Kings, which is why so little of the comment on them is particular to this book. He also notes the seizing and fortifying of that port as the act by which this able prince gave promise of his future at the outset of the reign, and probably completed the subjugation of Edom which his father had more than begun. Clarke supplies the chapter's shape in advance: the reign begins piously and prospers while the prophet lives, then come the campaigns against the Philistines, the Arabians and the Mehunims, the tribute of the Ammonites, the fortifying of Jerusalem and the towers in the country, the delight in husbandry, the account of the military strength and the engines, and then the elation of prosperity, the invasion of the priest's office, the leprosy, the abdication with his son acting as regent, and the burial.
5:
Who the prophet of the fifth verse was nobody can say, and all three admit as much. Gill clears away two candidates: not the last prophet but one, who lived three hundred years later, nor the Zechariah whom Joash slew, but perhaps a son of that one. Clarke says we know nothing of him but the character given him here, and infers that he was probably the young king's tutor. Ellicott calls him simply an otherwise unknown prophet.

What that character actually says divides them, because Ellicott will not keep the received text. The epithet rendered having understanding in the visions of God he translates as the skilled in seeing God, calls it a surprising phrase occurring nowhere else, and prefers the reading of some Hebrew manuscripts and of the Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Targum, which have the fear of God; this he judges doubtless correct, so that the clause should run that he gave instruction in the fear of God, as Rashi and Kimchi long since suggested. Clarke builds on the received reading, taking the visions of God for the true interpretation of divine prophecies, so that the prophet was wise in expounding them. Ellicott draws out what the relation amounted to: Zechariah was the guide and counsellor of the king, and not in religious matters only but in what we should call the political sphere, since the distinction between sacred and secular, civil and ecclesiastical, was then wholly unknown.

Ellicott also notices that the two histories substitute different judgments at this point. Where this writer accounts for the king's prosperity by his seeking God while the prophet lived, Kings makes the deduction usual in its estimate of a reign, that the high places were not taken away and the people still sacrificed on them. He adds that the construction rendered he sought God is really that he continued to seek, an expression peculiar to this writer.

On the campaigns the comment is mostly topography and consequence. Gill supplies the grievance behind the Philistine war, that they had broken in upon Judah in the days of Jehoram, and Ellicott agrees that the king assumed the offensive against peoples who had invaded under his predecessors. Ellicott identifies the towns: the wall of Gath was broken down after the city was taken; Jabneh is the Jamnia of the Maccabees and of Josephus, now a village some twelve miles south of Joppa; and Ashdod, like Gath one of the five sovereign states, commanded the great road to Egypt, which is why its possession mattered to the contending powers and why Sargon took it later. The phrase about Ashdod he reads as in Ashdod, the canton of that name, and judges the Philistines reduced to complete vassalage without annexation, since they continued under their own kings.

At the help of God two witnesses reach for the same Targum. Gill says the king did not do all this by his own strength but by the help of God, and reports the Targum rendering it that the Word of the Lord helped him; Clarke quotes the same rendering at greater length, with the Arabians living in Gerar and the plains of Meun, and identifies them with the Arabs called Meonites. Ellicott leaves the place-name open: Gur-Baal is mentioned only here and is unknown, the Targum making it Gerar and the Greek apparently Petra, while Gedor-Baal has been proposed; the Mehunims he takes for the people of Maon near Mount Seir. He records too that the Syriac and Arabic omit the stretch from the wall of Ashdod to the gifts of Uzziah. On those gifts all three agree that tribute is meant, Gill allowing that the Ammonites may have been merely desirous to live in friendship, Clarke making it an annual payment, and Ellicott noting that the king's influence reached the Egyptian border as Solomon's had, and that the closing verb means he made head.
9:
On the towers in the city Ellicott does the topography. The first commanded the gate at probably the north-west corner of the wall; the second stood in the western wall, at what is now the Jaffa gate; the third was over the angle east of Zion, where a bend let one tower defend both Zion and Moriah from the south-east. He also calls the English margin wrong on the last clause: the sense is not that the king fortified the gates but that he put the towers in a posture of defence. Gill supplies the history behind the first, that the corner gate had been broken down by the king of Israel in his father's time, so that Uzziah repaired and strengthened it with a tower.

The towers in the open country draw three readings of the same programme. Gill puts them in the desert of Arabia, to protect travellers from robbers and shepherds with their flocks. Clarke makes them a defence for the flocks and the shepherds. Ellicott reads the word as the grazing country west of the Dead Sea, makes the towers a guard for the royal herds, and renders the digging of wells as the hewing of cisterns to water them.

At Carmel the two part company over whether a place is meant at all. Clarke takes it for a place-name and reports from Calmet that there were two Carmels in Judea, one where Nabal lived and the other on the coast, both fertile in vines. Ellicott takes it for a common noun, the fruitful field or glebe land, and renders the closing clause literally, that a lover of the soil was he. Clarke turns that clause into a maxim and spends his longest note on it: this is a perfection in a king, since on husbandry every state depends, and whatever the trade there can be no true prosperity if agriculture does not, for the king himself is served by the field. Where a king encourages it the people cannot be reduced to wretchedness even should trade fail, because there is plenty of bread.

The muster is reported administratively by Ellicott and arithmetically by Gill. Ellicott notes that the host went out in organised troops with probably each house forming one, and that each chief led about a hundred and twenty men. Gill identifies the twenty-six hundred as the commanders and principal officers and observes that the army exceeded his father's by seven thousand five hundred besides officers. On the equipment Ellicott divides the list between the heavy armed, with shields and lances and helmets and coats of mail, and the light armed with bows and slings; Clarke reads the same provision as weapons held ready for the subjects' hands on any exigency.

The engines bring Gill and Clarke independently to the same claim of priority. Clarke calls this the first intimation on record of any warlike engine, long prior to anything of the kind among Greeks or Romans, and supports it from the consequences: before such inventions the besieged could only be starved out, so that sieges were long, Shalmaneser spending three years on so inconsiderable a place as Samaria and Sardanapalus holding Nineveh seven. Gill reaches the same conclusion by canvassing the rival claimants: these were what the Romans called catapults and ballistas, and by this it appears they were not first invented in Greece or Rome but in Judea; it is said the Romans had the battering machine from the Greeks and that the Trojan horse was no other than a battering ram, but if so the invention belongs rather to the Syrians and Phoenicians on Pliny's authority, or to the Carthaginians who were a colony of theirs; yet after all they seem the device of some skilful men among the Jews in Uzziah's time, and according to Diodorus Siculus they had not been found out when Nineveh was besieged.
16:
What the king was attempting is Ellicott's question, and his answer is the boldest thing in the chapter. Elevated by success, Uzziah appears to have wanted to be pontiff as well as king, holding the dual office the Egyptian rulers held. Some have thought he merely revived the precedent of David and Solomon; but Ellicott replies that it can hardly be proved those monarchs ever performed the distinctive functions of priests, and he points to the parallel of Saul. Gill supplies the occasion, that the strength which lifted him up was his victories, his dominions, his army and his fortified cities. Wesley fixes the place, the holy place where the altar of incense stood, into which none but priests might enter.

Whether the priests laid hands on him divides Gill from Wesley, and Ellicott's philology settles it. Gill has Azariah go in after the king to hinder him, and reads the withstanding as the priests not merely standing against him but standing about him, so that he could not approach the altar. Wesley denies force expressly, with a textual reason: they stood up against him not by laying hands on him, for in the next verse the censer is still in his hand, but only by admonition and reproof. Their warning he reads the same way: that it will not be for his honour means he should expect God to set some brand of infamy upon him. Ellicott comes down on Wesley's side, rendering the thrusting out as hurrying him away and noting that the word for his hasting is literally that he thrust himself.

On the leprosy as judgment Ellicott reports a reservation and a legend. The punishment, he notes, is the one that fell on Miriam and on Gehazi. Thenius, while granting the invasion of the sanctuary historical, holds that the chronicler followed traditional exegesis in making the leprosy a judgment on it; at all events, Ellicott answers, he gave the story as he found it in the history he refers to at the close. In Josephus the tale is embellished: the great earthquake the prophet mentions happened as the king threatened the priests, and a ray of sunlight falling on his face through a roof cloven by the shock produced the disease. Wesley reads the stroke as coming from beside the altar by an invisible hand, that he might be assured whose displeasure it was; and Gill observes it appeared in the forehead where all could see.

The seclusion is read as law, as medicine and as symmetry. Ellicott renders the several house as the hospital or lazar house, and notes that the reason given, that he was cut off from the house of the Lord, is this writer's addition. Clarke makes the separation total, from all society domestic, civil and religious, and has the son become regent because the father could no longer discharge the regal office. Wesley finds the pattern: God would have the leprosy incurable as a monument of his anger, and the punishment answered the sin as face answers face in a glass, since he thrust himself into the temple where only priests had admission and was for that thrust out of the courts into which the meanest subject might enter, invading a dignity to which he had no right and losing one to which he had an undoubted right.

At the close Clarke records a loss and a disgrace. The history Isaiah wrote of this king is totally lost, there being no account of him in Isaiah's writings, where he is barely mentioned; and as a leper he was refused the common burial place of the kings, since even a sepulture was supposed defiled by such a body. Gill dates the end, that on one chronologer's reckoning he died the same year he was struck, and that in the year of his death Isaiah saw his vision.
